title: AI compute provider Nscale is looking for $3.5B in pre-IPO financing
content:
Nscale, a British AI infrastructure company founded just two years ago, has said it may go public as early as later this month. Ahead of that expected IPO, the company is reportedly in talks to raise an additional $3.5 billion.
Bloomberg reported Friday that the company is looking to sell $1.5 billion in convertible notes — a type of loan that can later convert into company stock — to a group of investors, while also seeking an additional $2 billion in financing from Nvidia.
Nvidia also participated in the firm’s Series B funding round in March, a $1.1 billion raise led by investment fund Aker. Nscale hailed its round as “the largest Series B in European history.” The company’s Series A round, in December of 2024, raised $155 million.
TechCrunch reached out to Nscale and Nvidia for comment.
AI infrastructure startups have seen immense growth amid the current era of AI enthusiasm, wherein compute has become a competitive currency.
Nscale recently signed a large deal with Anthropic worth approximately $45 billion. Earlier this week, reports emerged that Nscale had been telling potential investors that it has approximately $103 billion in revenue following the deal. That figure isn’t current sales; it’s a projection based on signed customer leases, according to The Information.

report.summary: British AI compute startup Nscale may raise $3.5B pre-IPO, eyeing a public listing as early as this month amid surging AI infrastructure demand.
report.background: Nscale was founded only two years ago as a British provider of AI compute and cloud infrastructure. The category has exploded because advanced AI training and inference require expensive GPUs in huge quantities, making compute the most sought-after raw material of the current AI era. Nscale raised a $155M Series A in December 2024 and a $1.1B Series B in March 2026, reportedly the largest European Series B ever, led by investment fund Aker with participation from Nvidia. Now, ahead of a possible IPO in late September 2026, it seeks $1.5B in convertible notes plus an additional $2B from Nvidia. The company recently signed a deal with Anthropic worth approximately $45B, and has reportedly pitched investors on about $103B in revenue projections derived from signed customer leases, not current sales.
key_points: Nscale is raising $3.5B before an IPO, potentially combining $1.5B in convertible notes with $2B from Nvidia. This financing likely dilutes early investors but signals strong strategic backing. Convertible debt gives lenders upside while protecting downside, and Nvidia's participation shows deep alignment between the GPU maker and this young cloud provider.

Founded just two years ago, Nscale went from a $155M Series A in December 2024 to a $1.1B Series B in March 2026, called Europe's largest. Now it wants billions more pre-IPO. That trajectory underscores how AI compute startups are racing to secure data-center capacity and long-term GPU supply before competitors do.

Nscale sees potential $45B worth of business from Anthropic. After signing that deal, reports suggest Nscale has shown investors about $103B in future revenue based on signed leases. These are projected obligations, not current income, so valuation depends on assumptions about future GPU utilization and Anthropic staying committed.

Nvidia is doubling down. After taking part in Nscale's Series B, Nvidia is reportedly prepared to provide another $2B. That creates a flywheel where Nvidia finances GPU cloud customers and data centers, securing demand for its own hardware. Still, such relationships can create conflict when Nvidia also works with Nscale competitors like CoreWeave.

An IPO could arrive as early as this month or later in 2026. Public listing will test whether investors accept high valuations based on forward lease revenue for AI datacenters. It also gives retail investors exposure to what has been a private-market gold rush in compute capacity.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Nscale's financing push shows compute remains the defining constraint and investment focus. Nvidia's involvement suggests a consolidation era in which GPU makers fund their own customers, deepening ties and possibly squeezing independent cloud providers without similar backing. Developers and enterprises renting AI compute may benefit from more capacity, but a race toward tens of billions in capital raises could inflate infrastructure costs that pass through to users. Regular consumers will likely see indirect consequences: better availability of AI services if datacenters come online, or higher prices if overbuilding and debt create failures. For the broader ecosystem, Nscale's planned IPO is a canary, proving whether the public markets can absorb AI infrastructure mega-deals and forward-leasing valuations.
report.tools: If you want to explore AI compute infrastructure hands-on, watch open-source Kubernetes and KubeRay for distributed GPU workloads, Ray for scaling Python training, and the Slurm workload manager for HPC clusters. For monitoring GPU health, Nvidia's DCGM exporter with Prometheus is a standard combo. Note that Nscale's own software stack is proprietary, but these open tools run on most GPU clouds.
